In [[graph theory]], '''Grassmann graphs''' are a special class of [[simple graph]]s defined from systems of [[Linear subspace|subspace]]s. The [[vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] of the Grassmann graph {{math|''J''{{sub|''q''}}(''n'', ''k'')}} are the {{mvar|k}}-[[dimension (vector space)|dimension]]al subspaces of an {{mvar|n}}-dimensional [[vector space]] over a [[finite field]] of order {{mvar|q}}; two vertices are adjacent when their [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] is {{math|(''k'' − 1)}}-dimensional.

Many of the parameters of Grassmann graphs are [[Q-analog|{{mvar|q}}-analogs]] of the parameters of [[Johnson graph]]s, and Grassmann graphs have several of the same [[graph property|graph properties]] as Johnson graphs.

== Graph-theoretic properties ==

* {{math|''J''{{sub|''q''}}(''n'', ''k'')}} is [[Graph isomorphism|isomorphic]] to {{math|''J''{{sub|''q''}}(''n'', ''n'' − ''k'')}}.
* For all {{math|0 ≤ ''d'' ≤ diam(''J''{{sub|q}}(''n'',''k''))}}, the intersection of any pair of vertices at distance {{mvar|d}} is {{math|(''k'' − ''d'')}}-dimensional.
* The [[clique number]] of {{math|''J''{{sub|''q''}}(''n'',''k'')}} is given by an expression in terms its least and greatest [[eigenvalue]]s {{math|''λ''{{sub|&hairsp;min}}}} and {{math|''λ''{{sub|&hairsp;max}}}}:
::<math>\omega \left( J_q(n,k) \right) = 1 - \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}}</math>
{{Citation needed|date=November 2023}}

== Automorphism group ==
There is a [[Distance-transitive graph|distance-transitive]] [[subgroup]] of <math>\operatorname{Aut}(J_q(n, k))</math> [[group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to the [[projective linear group]] <math>\operatorname{P\Gamma L}(n, q)</math>.{{Citation needed|date=August 2024}}

In fact, unless <math>n = 2k</math> or <math>k \in \{ 1, n - 1 \}</math>, <math>\operatorname{Aut}(J_q(n,k)) \cong \operatorname{P\Gamma L}(n, q)</math>; otherwise <math>\operatorname{Aut}(J_q(n,k)) \cong \operatorname{P\Gamma L}(n, q) \times C_2</math> or <math>\operatorname{Aut}(J_q(n,k)) \cong \operatorname{Sym}([n]_q)</math> respectively.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Distance-Regular Graphs|last=Brouwer|first=Andries E.|date=1989|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|others=Cohen, Arjeh M., Neumaier, Arnold.|isbn=9783642743436|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|oclc=851840609}}</ref>

== Intersection array ==
As a consequence of being distance-transitive, <math>J_q(n,k)</math> is also [[Distance-regular graph|distance-regular]]. Letting <math>d </math> denote its [[Diameter (graph theory)|diameter]], the intersection array of <math>J_q(n,k)</math> is given by <math>\left\{ b_0, \ldots, b_{d-1}; c_1, \ldots c_d \right \} </math> where:
* <math>b_j := q^{2j + 1} [k - j]_q [n - k - j]_q </math> for all <math>0 \leq j < d </math>.
* <math>c_j := ([j]_q)^2 </math> for all <math>0 < j \leq d </math>.

== Spectrum ==
*The characteristic polynomial of <math>J_q(n,k)</math> is given by
:: <math>\varphi(x) := \prod\limits_{j=0}^{\operatorname{diam}(J_q(n, k))} \left ( x - \left ( q^{j+1} [k - j]_q [n - k - j]_q - [j]_q \right ) \right )^{\left ( \binom{n}{j}_q - \binom{n}{j-1}_q \right )}</math>.<ref name=":0" />
